You are a physician performing diagnostic reasoning on a published clinical case.

Case presentation:
An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a nodule on the palatal mucosa behind the right upper central incisor. Eight months earlier, he had sustained dental trauma with a crown fracture of that tooth without pulp exposure. On examination, there was a sessile‐based nodule, narrow in the anteroposterior dimension, with a smooth surface, slight white coloration, and diffuse posterior erythema; it was non‐tender on palpation. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed no bone involvement. Thermal sensitivity testing confirmed that the adjacent teeth were vital, effectively ruling out an acute or chronic periapical lesion.

Provide your diagnostic reasoning and final diagnosis.

1. Consideration of an acute or chronic periapical lesion — “thermal sensitivity testing confirmed that the teeth in the area were vital, ruling out an acute or chronic periapical lesion.” 2. Initial presumption of a parulis was excluded by vitality tests — “after ruling out the possibility of an endodontic origin of the lesion…” 3. Reactive lesions are common in young patients — “in the young population, reactive lesions seem to be the most recurrent differential diagnostic.” 4. Adult gingival cysts and peripheral odontogenic tumors are typical adult considerations — “in the adult population, adult gingival cyst and peripheral odontogenic tumors are the major differential diagnostic considerations; in the young population, reactive lesions seem…”

Final diagnosis: Extraosseous peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst
You are a physician performing diagnostic reasoning on a published clinical case.

Case presentation:
A 20-year-old man fell and struck the back of his head. He reported severe neck and shoulder pain with difficulty raising both arms and in gripping objects. He was alert (GCS 15), with normal vital signs and no signs of head injury or respiratory distress. On cervical palpation, there was tenderness at the upper cervical spine and marked paraspinal muscle spasm. Neurologically, he had weakness of both arms (right worse than left) in the C5–T1 distribution with brisk reflexes but no sensory deficits. The lower limbs had brisk reflexes but normal strength. Cranial nerves were intact. An open-mouth odontoid radiograph and cervical CT scan showed an undisplaced type III odontoid fracture.

Provide your diagnostic reasoning and final diagnosis.

1. Acute central cord syndrome was considered because of the selective upper-limb weakness after neck trauma, but was less likely given the association with odontoid fractures: “Acute CCS is rarely associated with injury to the atlanto–axial complex.” 2. Cruciate paralysis was considered because it presents with arm paralysis and minimal or absent lower-limb involvement in the setting of upper cervical injury, and is often linked to axis fractures: “Cruciate paralysis has been closely associated with fractures of axis and/or atlas.”

Final diagnosis: cruciate paralysis

normal.
You may gently wash away dried material around your incision.
Avoid direct sun exposure to the incision area.
Do not use any ointments on the incision unless you were told

your surgeon.

Constipation is a common side effect of narcotic pain 
medicaitons. If needed, you may take a stool softener (such as 
Colace, one capsule) or gentle laxative (such as milk of 
magnesia, 1 tbs) twice a day. You can get both of these 
medicines without a prescription.
If you go 48 hours without a bowel movement, or have pain moving 
the bowels, call your surgeon.

It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal 
surgery. This pain is often described as "soreness". 
Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain is

You will receive a prescription for pain medicine to take by 
mouth. It is important to take this medicine as directed. Do not 
take it more frequently than prescribed. Do not take more 
medicine at one time than prescribed. Do not drink alcohol or 
drive while taking narcotic pain medication.
Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before your 
pain gets too severe.

prescription pain medicine. Please don't take any other pain 
medicine, including non-prescription pain medicine, unless your 
surgeon has said its okay.

pain medicine.

- pain that is getting worse over time
- pain accompanied by fever of more than 101
- a drastic change in nature or quality of your pain

take, please call your surgeon.

Context:
Sources of reports about laparoscopic and percutaneous treatment of liver hydatid cysts are limited to just a few countries. To address the reason behind this, we carried out a survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan. A questionnaire was distributed to collect data regarding the surgical technique preferred by each surgeon. Further information was collected from those not adopting minimal-access techniques to determine their reasons for not doing so. Only 3 surgeons (10%) considered laparoscopy as the first line of treatment. Of the 27 surgeons who did not consider percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment, fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination was the main reason given by 21 surgeons (78%) for not using minimal access techniques.

Question: Is fear of anaphylactic shock discouraging surgeons from more widely adopting percutaneous and laparoscopic techniques in the treatment of liver hydatid cyst?
Yes. The seemingly exaggerated traditional fear of anaphylaxis seems to discourage surgeons from more widely adopting minimal access techniques for the treatment of hydatid cyst.
